The Polish footprints of Istanbul, on foot

A map and pocket guide to 38 places where Poles left their mark on Istanbul – from Adampol, the Polish village in the forests above the Bosphorus, to the house where Adam Mickiewicz died, the gates through which the Commonwealth's envoys rode to the sultan and the quay where Poland's gold passed through in 1939. Nine chapters of Polish history

Istanbul has a Polish story, and most visitors walk straight past it. More than six centuries of Polish–Turkish history, told place by place. Every place on the map belongs to one of these themes.

Adampol – Polonezköy

The Polish village founded in 1842 at Prince Adam Czartoryski's wish in the forests of Beykoz: its church, its cemetery, “Aunt Zosia's House”, the memorial of Atatürk's visit and the nature park.

The Great Emigration and Mickiewicz

The museum on the spot where Adam Mickiewicz died in November 1855, the church where the exiles were granted the land for Adampol, and the graves of General Langiewicz and Tadeusz Gasztowtt.

Poles in the Sultan's service

Michał Czajkowski, the novelist who became Sadyk Pasha; Stanisław Chlebowski, court painter to Sultan Abdülaziz; and Wojciech Bobowski – Ali Ufkî – who grew up in the palace school of Topkapı.

Envoys and diplomacy

The inn where the Commonwealth's great embassies lodged, the Sublime Porte, the audience halls of Topkapı and the old “Polish Street” off İstiklal.

Wars and captivity

Khotyn 1621 and the tomb of Osman II, the Yedikule fortress where Polish nobles were held, Kara Mustafa Pasha of Vienna 1683 and the site of the old slave market.

Roxelana

Hürrem Sultan, wife of Süleyman the Magnificent, whom Polish tradition places in Rohatyn: her tomb, the bathhouse Sinan built for her and her first great foundation.

Churches, cemeteries and John Paul II

St Anthony's Basilica with its Sunday Mass in Polish, Santa Maria Draperis, the Cathedral of the Holy Spirit and the stops of John Paul II's visit in November 1979.

1939–1945

In September 1939 the gold reserves of the Bank of Poland passed through Istanbul: from a British ship anchored off Kabataş to a train at Haydarpaşa bound for Beirut.

Polish Istanbul today

The villagers of Polonezköy, the Polish Mass at St Anthony's and the Consulate General in Maslak, today's address of Polish diplomacy on the Bosphorus.

What's inside

Every place sits on the map, grouped by theme. Tap it for the story, the pictures, the people involved and a short note on visiting.

38 places with their stories

Churches and cemeteries, palace gates and audience halls, a village, a museum, a railway station and a quay – each with its story, period, district, sources and a note on visiting. Where a story rests on tradition rather than documents, the text says so.

Eight walks

Each walk links places that belong to one story. The times are rough guides for walking and looking, without museum visits.

  1. Mickiewicz's Pera Free

    6 stops · about 2 h 45 min · from Galata to Feriköy, with the Tünel funicular and the metro

  2. Sadyk Pasha and the Sultan's Painter Free

    2 stops · about 1 h 30 min · downhill from Cihangir to Dolmabahçe on the Bosphorus

  3. Adampol: a Polish Village by the Bosphorus

    9 stops · about 2 h · on foot through the village, which you reach by taxi or bus

  4. Sultans and Envoys

    9 stops · about 3 h · the old city, from the Column of Constantine to Topkapı Palace

  5. In Roxelana's Footsteps

    3 stops · about 2 h · Haseki, the Süleymaniye and Sultanahmet

  6. Khotyn and the Seven Towers

    2 stops · about 2 h 30 min · Sultanahmet and Yedikule, by tram or Marmaray

  7. The 1939 Gold and the General

    3 stops · about 2 h 30 min · Kabataş, then by ferry to Kadıköy and Haydarpaşa

  8. John Paul II in Istanbul, 1979

    4 stops · about 3 h 30 min · Harbiye, İstiklal, Fener and Kumkapı, by public transport

Opening hours change – each place in the app tells you what to check before you go.

Questions and answers

Is this a self-guided walking tour of Polish Istanbul?

Yes. The eight walks are self-guided routes with numbered stops and a story at each one. You walk at your own pace, and the app hands the stops to Apple Maps or Google Maps for directions.

Which places are in the app?

38 places linked to Polish history in Istanbul, for example the village of Polonezköy (Adampol) with its church and cemetery, the Adam Mickiewicz Museum, St Anthony's Basilica on İstiklal, the Sublime Porte and the audience halls of Topkapı Palace, the Yedikule fortress, the tomb and bathhouse of Hürrem Sultan (Roxelana), Haydarpaşa station, the grave of General Langiewicz and the Ecumenical Patriarchate, where John Paul II prayed in 1979.

Does it work offline?

The stories and all the pictures are inside the app and work without a connection. The street map comes from OpenStreetMap and directions open in your maps app; both need mobile data or Wi-Fi.

What is free, and what does the unlock include?

The map, a first look at every place and two complete walks in and around Pera – “Mickiewicz's Pera” and “Sadyk Pasha and the Sultan's Painter” – are free. One purchase unlocks all 38 stories, all 8 walks, every picture, directions to every place and future content updates.

Is it a subscription?

No. It is a one-time purchase, with no ads and no account. On another iPhone or iPad, or after reinstalling, tap “Restore purchases” with the same Apple Account.

Which languages does it speak?

Polish, English and Turkish – every story is written in all three. The app starts in your phone's language (English if it is none of the three), and you can switch in Settings.

Do I need to be in Istanbul to use it?

No. You can read the stories and plan your walks at home. Distances and the “you are here” dot appear once you are in the city and allow location access.

Does the app track me?

No. There is no account, no advertising and no tracking. The app sends anonymous usage statistics that you can switch off in Settings; the privacy policy lists exactly what they contain.

How do I get to Polonezköy (Adampol)?

The village lies on the Asian side, in the forests of Beykoz, about 25 km from Sultanahmet as the crow flies. There is no rail or metro: the simplest way is a taxi from Kavacık or Beykoz (about 15–20 minutes). City buses also run there – check the current lines before you set off. The village itself can be walked in about two hours; weekdays are much quieter than weekends.
